say.text: A 40-year-old man has hereditary spherocytosis, chronic haemolysis and gallstones. Which stone is he most likely to have, and where does it form?

choices.label: Brown pigment stones, formed in the bile ducts
Black pigment stones, formed in the bile ducts
Black pigment stones, formed in the gallbladder
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Chronic haemolysis is the clue: black stones are small, multiple and hard, form in the gallbladder, and go with cirrhosis.
That is not the right choice.
It tempts because the pigment name is familiar, and the ducts feel like the place where stones cause trouble.
But brown stones are soft and earthy, and go with infected bile and stasis, not with haemolysis.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so pair the cause with the stone: haemolysis does not point to the soft, infected-bile stone.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
It tempts because black stones are the haemolysis stone, so the site can slip when you read the stem.
But stones that form in infected ducts are the soft, earthy type, and that does not match a haemolysis picture.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so split the site from the colour: duct stones in infection are soft and earthy.

say.text: Start with the cause the stem gives you: red cells breaking down early. Which stone goes with that, and what is it like?
Black pigment stones are small, multiple and hard, form in the gallbladder, and go with haemolysis and cirrhosis.
Brown pigment stones are soft and earthy, form in infected bile in the ducts, and bacterial enzymes help make them.
A man with Ascaris and recurrent cholangitis has soft, earthy stones removed from his bile ducts. Which stone type, and where did it form?

choices.label: Brown pigment stones, formed in the gallbladder
Brown pigment stones, formed in the bile ducts
Black pigment stones, formed in the gallbladder
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Look at the cause the stem gives you: a parasite and repeated infection. Which pigment is tied to infection, not to haemolysis?
That is not the right choice.
It tempts because the gallbladder is where most stones are first imagined, so the site feels like the default.
But brown stones need bacterial enzymes in infected bile to form, so ask where that infected bile sits.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the site separately from the pigment: the infection clue points to where infected bile stagnates.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
It tempts because the gallbladder is the usual home of a pigment stone, and black stones do form there.
But black stones go with haemolysis and cirrhosis, and this stem gives a worm and repeated cholangitis instead.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so pair each pigment with its cause: black with haemolysis, not with worms and cholangitis.

say.text: Yes. Brown pigment stones are soft and earthy, form in the bile ducts, and go with infection and stasis.
The worm and the cholangitis are the infection link, and bacterial enzymes in infected bile favour this stone.
Cholesterol stones have their own risk factors. Think female, fat, fertile and forty, often with fair added.
Oestrogens and pregnancy raise biliary cholesterol, and obesity or rapid weight loss add to the risk.
Which of these is a risk factor for cholesterol stones?

choices.label: Chronic haemolysis, as in hereditary spherocytosis
Cirrhosis of the liver, long-standing disease
Oral contraceptive use, raising biliary cholesterol
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think of the female and hormone clues in the mnemonic, and of body fat and weight, not of the blood or the liver.
That is not the right choice.
It tempts because haemolysis was the cause in your first case, so it sticks to the stone question.
But chronic haemolysis goes with black pigment stones, not with cholesterol stones.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so keep the haemolysis stone apart from the cholesterol risk factors.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
It tempts because liver disease feels like a whole-body cause that reaches the whole biliary tree.
But cirrhosis is the link to black pigment stones, while cholesterol stones follow hormones, fat and weight.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so match cirrhosis to black stones, and the cholesterol risks to hormones and weight.

say.text: Yes. Oral contraceptives raise biliary cholesterol secretion and reduce gallbladder motility, so they add to cholesterol stones.
Compare acute cholecystitis with a stone (calculous) and without one (acalculous). Which is true of the acalculous form?

choices.label: Has more gangrene, perforation and higher mortality
Runs a milder course, as no stone obstructs
Has lower mortality, as patients are younger
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think about the patient, not the stone. What happens to blood flow and bile flow in a critically ill patient?
That is not the right choice.
It tempts because a stone is the usual trigger, so no stone sounds like a safer course.
But this form starts from stasis and ischaemia in critically ill patients, so no stone does not mean milder.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the mechanism: stasis and ischaemia drive this disease, not the stone.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
It tempts because younger patients usually do better after surgery and infection.
But this form strikes sick patients after burns, sepsis or major surgery, so age is not the driver.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check who gets this disease: the critically ill.

say.text: Yes. Acalculous disease comes from stasis and ischaemia in critically ill patients, so gangrene, perforation and mortality run higher.
A burns patient on day four in the intensive care unit (ICU) has fever and right upper quadrant (RUQ) pain. Ultrasound shows no stone. What should you plan around?

choices.label: Low risk, since no stone is present
Gangrene and perforation risk is high
Mild, safe to observe without imaging
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Set aside whether a stone is present. What does a critically ill patient's gallbladder suffer from, and what can that do to its wall?
That is not the right choice.
It tempts because stones are the usual danger in this organ, so a stone-free scan looks reassuring.
But stasis and ischaemia in a burns patient can damage the wall with no stone at all.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so remember that a stone-free gallbladder can still be the sick one.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
It tempts because many gallbladder patients settle, and a quiet picture seems safe.
But this disease is driven by ischaemia in a sick patient, and it runs a worse course, not a milder one.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the severity in this group before you decide to watch.

say.text: Yes. In a critically ill patient, stasis and ischaemia can gangrene or perforate the wall without any stone.
No stone means no obstruction, yet the wall still fails from stasis and ischaemia. This form is about 5 to 10 per cent of cases.
Its gangrene, perforation and mortality run higher than in calculous disease, so a stone-free label never means safe.
